newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: CRICKET-SA COACH QUERIES LIKELY CHANGES IN CONTEST.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-SA COACH QUERIES LIKELY CHANGES IN CONTEST.

text.p: National coach Bob Woolmer and former test captain Kepler Wessels have mixed feelings about suggested changes to South Africa's domestic first-class cricket competition.

South Africa's 2-1 loss to Australia in their home test series earlier this year prompted several calls for an immediate restructuring of the four-day Supersport Series in an attempt to lessen the step-up to cricket at the highest level.

It was believed by many that nine teams in the country's premier domestic tournament diluted player strength and that a return to the old Currie Cup system of two divisions of five or six sides each -- with promotion and relegation -- was desirable.
South African coach Bob Woolmer is in favour of two divisions of six teams, but with one major reservation.

"Two sections of six and six, with promotion and relegation, would give every side five games -- both home and away -- during the season. And that would be better than how it is now," he told Reuters.

"But, if you do that, you'll inherit the transfer system that you have in soccer and teams in the second division would be weakened because their players would be bought up by the stronger provinces."
Former South African captain and present Eastern Province skipper Kepler Wessels feels that, whatever form of domestic competition is adopted, playing standards will be weakened.
"The bottom line is, with international commitments these days, you're going to have weakened teams. You're never going to get a strong domestic competition.

"The standard will always be a bit low, whether you've got six or eight teams in your domestic set-up. And it's a two-edged sword. Obviously the higher the standard of your domestic cricket, the less of a jump-up you get to test level," Wessels said.

"When I played in Australia's Sheffield Shield, it was considered the strongest first-class competition in the world and even there you had weakened sides. It's not a system that you can really solve."
Woolmer believes one bonus with the present system is that players from the likes of Griqualand West, Boland and Border enjoy the exposure of playing against the top players in the country.

"Next year our international players won't be playing in any of the Supersport Series matches. We're away from September 25 to February 4 and then we have the home series against Pakistan and Sri Lanka," he said.

"It's vital that we broaden the base of the game in this country, so that more players build up to the Supersport Series. We've got to have more games and more teams to give players from the disadvantaged areas the chance to come through and to shine on a bigger platform. At the moment, the base is too small.

"The South African side which competed at the under-15 World Cup in England last year had five players from the disadvantaged areas but to expect even one of the five to come through is pushing it really. We need a large pool of players to choose from."
Woolmer wants to see under-19 sides playing in their own version of the Supersport Series.
"Four different competitions would be ideal. A provincial A section, a B section, an under-19 section and an under-17 competition. The under-18s are already taen care of."
